definition: To formally approve an agreement or decision so that it becomes official.
example: The hiking club gathered at the lodge to ratify its new trail-safety rules.
nuance: To ratify is to give official approval to something already drafted, usually by a group with authority; do not confuse it with rectify, to fix.
prompt: Members of a neighborhood garden association meet to review bylaws written by a committee.
options: After a short debate, the members voted to ratify the committee's bylaws.
Before the meeting, a volunteer tried to ratify the broken gate by nailing a new board across it.
The members chose to ratify the bylaws, so the whole proposal was rejected and thrown out.
One gardener decided to ratify the bylaws quietly by skimming them alone in her kitchen.
reasons: A group with authority voting to make a drafted document official is exactly what this verb describes.
Repairing something is rectifying it; this sentence mixes up two similar-sounding words.
Giving official approval cannot also mean rejecting; the sentence reverses the meaning.
Reading something privately is not a formal act of approval, and one person here has no power to make it official.

practice.prompt: The board of a youth soccer league considers a schedule agreement worked out with a nearby league.
options: On Monday the board met to ratify the schedule that the two leagues had negotiated.
At halftime the coach shouted to ratify his players so they would run faster in the second half.
The board chose to ratify the agreement by refusing to sign it and sending it back unchanged.
A curious goalie wanted to ratify the new schedule by asking a teammate what dates it listed.
reasons: The governing board officially confirms a deal that was negotiated beforehand, which is the correct use.
The word has nothing to do with motivating or energizing people.
Refusing to sign is a rejection, the opposite of making an agreement official.
Asking about a document is not approving it, and a single player has no authority to make it official.
